name: The ultimate in the Tamil Siddha songs (Civam, Parāparam, the Light, the open space)

definitions.definition: The Siddhars name the ultimate Civam, Parāparam, Paramporuḷ, the Light (cōti, parañcōti) and the open space (veṭṭa veḷi). It is within the body and everywhere, self-luminous, the undivided fullness (akaṇṭa paripūraṇam), identical with love (TM 270), beyond qualities and beyond what devotees can speak; it is found by inner knowledge and the guru's grace, not in stone images, temples or scripture.

relations.note: Tāyumāṉavar describes it as light, fullness of bliss and grace, close to the Vedāntic triad

definitions.definition: The boundless open space above and beyond the body's supports, taken as the truth itself: for those who hold it true no title-deed is needed (Kuṭampai 1); the heart 'standing empty' without ritual (Aḻukaṇṇi 37); 'the open space of pure Vedānta' (Kaṭuveḷi 10).

relations.note: not to be identified with Buddhist emptiness; verbal resemblance only

definitions.definition: The goddess as a young girl (Vālai, Bālā), 'mother Maṉōṉmaṇi, the supreme light', worshipped at the root with three syllables and on the Meru of forty-three triangles; she stands in the state beyond qualities.

relations.note: Caṭṭaimuṉi's Meru of 43 triangles is the Śrīcakra; Vālai is Bālā Tripurasundarī of Śrīvidyā

definitions.definition: Tāyumāṉavar's 'harmony' of Vedānta and Śaiva Siddhānta: the Siddhas who have attained it are praised; the Supreme is both the non-dual reality and the Lord of grace. Kaṭuveḷi likewise joins 'pure Vedānta' to Śiva devotion.
Vallalar (Ramalinga Swamigal) takes up camaracam in the name of his 'Camaraca Cutta Caṉmārkkam'.

relations.note: Siddhānta's own 'advaita of inseparability' is one pole of the harmony

name: The letters a and u (akāram, ukāram)

definitions.definition: The letter 'a' is the root, foot and crown of all and the Supreme itself (taṟparam); 'u' is supreme consciousness (ciṟparam); together they are He and She. Kaṭuveḷi's 'knowing the eight and the two' is read as a and u in Tamil numerals (code language).

relations.note: a and u are the first two elements of Om

name: The self in the Siddhar songs (āṉmā, uyir)

definitions.definition: The soul (āṉmā, uyir) plays the body's play and leaves it to wither (Kaṭuveḷi 21); the house of nine openings is not 'I' (Pattirakiriyār 39); the seeker asks 'who am I, who are you' (225) and longs to stand as 'I am He' (219); to know oneself is to join the Lord (Kuṭampai 31).

name: Mind and senses in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: The four inner faculties (maṉam, putti, cittam, akaṅkāram) form a 'fourfold fort' to be seized; the five senses are thieves whose forest must be burnt (Kaṭuveḷi 14); the mind is a demon (akappēy) and a fish in a net, to be stilled.

relations.note: karaṇam 4 and pulaṉ 5 are among the 96

definitions.definition: Among the ninety-six principles: waking (cākkiram), dream (coppaṉam), deep sleep (cuḻutti), the fourth (turiyam) and beyond the fourth (turiyātītam). The songs add 'sleeping without sleeping' and the blissful awareness that needs no further knowledge (Kuṭampai 15).

relations.note: the same five names as in Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta

definitions.definition: The unceasing 'sleep of Śiva-yoga' in which the senses are burnt away and awareness remains (Pattirakiriyār 1–2); 'for those whose sleep is destroyed and who remain in awareness, why seals?' (Kuṭampai 6).

relations.note: a sleep-like absorption with awareness

definitions.definition: Simply being still — the silent guru's whole teaching to Tāyumāṉavar; stilling the mind is harder than every power (taming elephants, transmuting metals, entering other bodies).

name: The ninety-six principles

definitions.definition: The Siddha and Siddha-medical enumeration of the embodied person (toṇṇūṟṟāṟu tattuvam), in the commonly given form: elements 5, sense-organs 5, sense-objects 5, organs of action 5, their functions 5, inner faculties 4, knowing (aṟivu) 1, channels (nāṭi) 10, winds (vāyu) 10, receptacles (ācayam) 5, sheaths (kōcam) 5, supports (ātāram) 6, circles (maṇṭalam) 3, impurities (malam) 3, humours (tōṣam) 3, desires (ēṭaṇai) 3, qualities (kuṇam) 3, deeds (viṉai) 2, passions (irākam) 8, states (avattai) 5 = 96. Aḻukaṇṇi speaks of 'the ninety and six' (19) and of all the principles burnt in realization (36).
The same count is the anatomical base of Siddha medicine: health and disease are read against the ninety-six.

relations.note: Śaiva Siddhānta's 36 are the cosmic principles; the 96 enumerate the embodied person
the first 24–25 of the 96 overlap the Sāṃkhya principles

notes: The overall count is certain; the membership given is the one most often printed, recalled at low confidence — some lists include the nine openings (vācal 9) and differ elsewhere. The Varāha Upaniṣad has its own 96.

definitions.definition: The six supports (āṟu ātāram) — mūlātāram, cuvātiṭṭāṉam, maṇipūrakam, anākatam, vicutti, ākkiñai — with the crown-space above; the goddess and the fire at the root; the guru's grace burns them away with the fifty-one letters (Aḻukaṇṇi 35).
Ten principal nāṭis among the ninety-six: iṭakalai, piṅkalai, cuḻumuṉai, kāntāri, atti, cikuvai, alampuṭai, puruṭaṉ, caṅkiṉi, kuku (Tamil forms; list recalled at moderate confidence).
Ten winds among the ninety-six: pirāṇaṉ, apāṉaṉ, viyāṉaṉ, utāṉaṉ, camāṉaṉ, nākaṉ, kūrmaṉ, kirukaraṉ, tēvatattaṉ, taṉañcayaṉ; in medicine they are the ten forms of the vātam humour.
Siddha medicine treats the ten vāyus as the subdivisions of vaḷi (vātam).
Tamil kuṇṭali: the coiled power at the root, in whose seat Guha is invoked; roused by the guru, it passes the six supports through the central channel to the moon of nectar.
Five kōcams among the ninety-six: aṉṉamayam, pirāṇamayam, maṉōmayam, viññāṉamayam, āṉantamayam.

name: The three circles (maṇṭalam) of fire, sun and moon

definitions.definition: Among the ninety-six: the circles of fire (akkiṉi), sun (ñāyiṟu) and moon (tiṅkaḷ) in the body, from root to head; the moon's nectar flows from the highest.
The breath, 'the horse that rose with twelve feet', is to be bound and nourished; mastered in vāci yoga it makes the body endure (TM 722; Caṭṭaimuṉi 4; Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 17). Summary only.

relations.note: vāci is the breath considered as the yogin's mount

definitions.definition: For the Siddhars the Lord has made the body his temple (TM 725); the heart is the sanctum and the flesh the shrine (TM 1823); temple and sacred tank are within the mind (Sivavākkiyar) — hence both the care of the body and the scorn for stone temples.

What is in the cosmos is in the body and the reverse; the Lord fills both (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam invocation). This is the ground on which the Siddhars read the body's supports, circles and channels as a cosmos.

name: The three humours (mukkuṟṟam: vaḷi, aḻal, aiyam)

definitions.definition: Vaḷi (vātam), aḻal (pittam) and aiyam (kapam), the 'three reckoned by the learned beginning with wind', whose excess or deficiency causes disease (Kuṟaḷ 941). Each has subdivisions (vātam 10 — the ten winds; pittam 5; kapam 5). The Tirumantiram's rejuvenating practice removes aiyam, vātam and pittam at their times of day.

relations.note: functionally the Āyurvedic tridoṣa; the Siddha tradition claims its own origin (see dsp:siddha-ayurveda-relation)

definitions.definition: Cāram (chyle/plasma), ceṉnīr (blood), ūṉ (flesh), koḻuppu (fat), eṉpu (bone), mūḷai (marrow), cukkilam / curōṇitam (semen / ovum), nourished in succession and governed by the humours.

relations.note: the Āyurvedic seven dhātus

definitions.definition: Nilam (earth), nīr (water), tī (fire), vaḷi (air), viṇ / ākāyam (ether): the body and every drug are made of them; the humours are compounded of them — vaḷi of air (and ether), aḻal of fire, aiyam of earth and water.
Cāttuvikam, irācatam, tāmatam — the three qualities (kuṇam) among the ninety-six principles.

Sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter and astringent, each formed of two elements, increasing or decreasing the humours; every drug is known by taste, potency (vīriyam), post-digestive effect (pirivu) and action (ceykai).

Pulse, touch, tongue, colour, voice, eyes, stool and urine are examined to find the disease, its cause and its remedy — after Kuṟaḷ 948–949: examine the disease, its cause, the means of allaying it, the patient, the measure of the illness and the time.

name: Pulse reading (nāṭi)

definitions.definition: The pulse at the wrist is felt with three fingers for vātam, pittam and kapam; in health their beats are said to stand in the ratio one : half : quarter (mātrai). Pulse is the first and chief examination.

notes: Ratio and finger placement recalled at moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: The urine is examined for colour, density, smell, froth and deposit (nīrkkuṟi), and by a drop of oil placed on it (neykkuṟi): spreading like a snake shows vātam, like a ring pittam, standing like a pearl kapam.

name: The 4,448 diseases

definitions.definition: The Siddha tradition counts 4,448 diseases, classified by humour and organ; the classification is usually credited to Agastya.

notes: The count is the tradition's standard figure; which text first gives it is not recalled (low).

name: The three classes of Siddha drugs

definitions.definition: Plants (mūlikai), minerals and metals (tātu) and animal products (jīvam); plant drugs act slowest and gentlest, mineral-metal drugs fastest and most potent, in the tradition's own ranking.

name: Forms of medicine: 32 internal and 32 external

definitions.definition: The tradition counts thirty-two internal forms (e.g. juice, decoction kuṭinīr, powder cūraṇam, electuary lēkiyam, medicated ghee and oil, pill kuḷikai, waxy meḻuku, calcined parpam, centūram, cuṇṇam, kaṭṭu) and thirty-two external forms (e.g. poultice, fomentation, oil application, fumigation, collyrium, nasal drops, massage tokkaṇam, leech and cautery). Treatment involves patient, physician, medicine and attendant (Kuṟaḷ 950) and a regimen of restrictions (pattiyam).

notes: Only examples are listed; the full 32+32 lists are not recalled.

name: Metal and mineral preparations (parpam, centūram) — names and warnings only

definitions.definition: Calcined metal and mineral medicines — parpam (white calx), centūram (red calx), cuṇṇam, kaṭṭu, meḻuku — held by the tradition to be the most potent Siddha medicines. The tradition's own warnings: raw minerals and metals are poison; they must be purified (cutti) and processed exactly as the guru teaches; wrongly made they kill; they are given only with strict regimen (pattiyam) and by a qualified physician. No processes, ingredients or doses are recorded here.

name: The poisonous minerals (pāṣāṇam) and the nine of Palani

definitions.definition: The tradition counts sixty-four pāṣāṇams, thirty-two natural and thirty-two prepared; Bogar is said to have made the Palani image of Murukaṉ from nine (navapāṣāṇam). Recorded as the tradition's account; no identities or processing.

name: Muppu, the secret salt of the alchemists

definitions.definition: The 'three salts', named as the key to fixing mercury, to transmutation and to making the body last for aeons (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 17); its composition is deliberately veiled in code language and to be learned only from a guru. Summary only.
Six seasons of the year and six divisions of the day, taken from Tamil poetics, govern the rise and fall of the humours and the timing of treatment; the physician must weigh the time (Kuṟaḷ 949).

Points where life-breath concentrates; 108 in the Siddha count (12 paṭu, 96 toṭu varmam); used in healing (varma maruttuvam) and in the martial art; ascribed to Agastya. Summary only; no locations or techniques.

relations.note: Āyurveda's marmas: related idea, different count

definitions.definition: Without the body life perishes and true knowledge cannot be reached; knowing the means to nourish the body, one nourishes the life (TM 724); the Lord has made the body his temple (TM 725). Kāya citti removes karma and opens higher powers (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 14); vāci yoga makes it free of obstacles (Caṭṭaimuṉi 4).

relations.note: as means, in TM 724

definitions.definition: Herbal, breath, yogic and mineral-metal regimens to make the body firm, reverse grey hair and wrinkles (TM 727) and prolong life for yoga. The tradition warns that mineral and mercurial kaṟpam without a guru is deadly; and Kuṭampai asks what need of kaṟpam the true knower has (2).
In Siddha medicine kaṟpam is the rejuvenative branch (kaṟpa maruttuvam).

relations.note: Āyurveda's rasāyana

definitions.definition: The Siddhar ideal of dying to death while living: 'this root makes one die without dying' (Rāmatēvar 2); leaving the fatal fruit to 'die without dying' (Aḻukaṇṇi 9); crossing over without dying (Kuṭampai 13); knowers have no Yama (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 10).

relations.note: liberation while living, in the idiom of conquering death

definitions.definition: The tradition holds that the Siddhars did not die: they live on in subtle or perfected bodies in the Potiyil, Caturakiri and Kolli hills, abide in their samādhi shrines, fly and travel far (Bogar to China), enter other bodies (Tirumūlar) and vanish into liṅgas (Paṭṭiṉattār). Recorded as the tradition's account.

A Siddhar enters samādhi and is enclosed alive, remaining present at the shrine; the eighteen have such shrines in the popular list (Palani, Chidambaram, Tiruvaṇṇāmalai…). Recorded as belief; no practice details.

name: Death and impermanence in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: The body is a bubble on water (Kaṭuveḷi 3), a leaking pot of salt (Aḻukaṇṇi 8), a hard-won pot broken in play (Kaṭuveḷi 4); nothing comes at birth or goes at death (Paṭṭiṉattār 7); kin and wealth do not last, only the Lord's feet (13); even an eyeless needle will not come on the last road; Yama comes tomorrow.

name: Testing the span of life (āyuḷ parīṭcai) and the wheel of time

definitions.definition: The Tirumantiram's third tantra has sections on the wheel of time (kāla cakkaram) and the testing of the remaining life-span (āyuḷ parīṭcai), by which the yogin reads the approach of death; Siddha lore uses them.

relations.note: yogic signs of approaching death

notes: Section titles checked in the local TM e-text; contents not summarized.

name: Karma and rebirth in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: Most Siddhar voices take rebirth under the two deeds for granted — 'how many mothers, how many births' (Paṭṭiṉattār), the Lord drives us by the rope of the two deeds (Tiruttillai 11), one's own deed burns oneself — while a famous Sivavākkiyar verse says the dead are not born again. Burning the old fate ends the two deeds (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 13).

name: Liberation (vīṭu, mutti) in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: Release is knowing the root (Kaṭuveḷi 13), seeing the 'house' once the senses are burnt (14), standing as 'I am He' (Pattirakiriyār 219), the heart left empty in the open space; it is reached in this body — perfected and deathless for some, seen through as a pot of filth for others — by the guru's grace, devotion (Kaṭuveḷi 18) and never forgetting the Lord's feet (Tiruttillai 16).

relations.note: release in this body

name: The four pādas: caryā, kriyā, yoga, jñāna

definitions.definition: The Tirumantiram's four paths (caryai, kiriyai, yōkam, ñāṉam) are accepted by Tāyumāṉavar and underlie the Siddhars' view that outer worship belongs to the lower rungs, which the knower leaves behind.

name: The eight lordly powers (aṇimā and the rest)

definitions.definition: Tamil aṭṭamā citti — aṇimā, makimā, lakimā, karimā, pirātti, pirākāmiyam, īcattuvam, vacittuvam — taught in the Tirumantiram's third tantra and claimed by the Siddhars; Tāyumāṉavar ranks them below stilling the mind and Kaṭuveḷi says they come only by Śiva's action.

The Siddhars veil yoga, alchemy and medicine in coded names and riddles — the house of three-times-two, the horse of twelve feet, the root tamarind, the eight and the two — so that only a guru's disciple can decode them; glossaries such as the Akattiyar paripāṣai explain some. The veiling is itself a warning against misuse.

relations.note: the 'intentional/twilight language' of the Buddhist siddhas: comparable device

name: Mantra and sound in the Siddhar songs

definitions.definition: The five letters bring birthless release (Paṭṭiṉattār); the three syllables of Vālai are uttered at the root (Rāmatēvar 2); the fifty-one letters are burnt by the guru (Aḻukaṇṇi 35); yet 'for those in the true tantra, why mantra?' (Kuṭampai 7) and the highest mantra is the unspoken one (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).

Do no sin (Kaṭuveḷi pallavi); no slander, lying, cursing, anger or cruelty, not even stones thrown at birds; no killing or flesh-eating; no ganja, opium or toddy; no false garb; give away the wealth Śiva gave; wish that all beings be happy (Tāyumāṉavar). One Siddhar also enjoins the Veda's rule (Kaṭuveḷi 8).
Caste has no basis: no difference in flesh, skin and bone between a Paṟaicci and a Brahmin woman (Sivavākkiyar); the castes called unequal are one (Kaṭuveḷi 32); 'one family, one God' (TM 2104).

relations.note: parallel critique in the vacanas

name: The Siddhar critique of images and ritual

definitions.definition: The planted stone does not speak (Sivavākkiyar); chiselled stone, moulded image and polished copper are not the Real (Pattirakiriyār 16); realization comes without ablutions or flowers (Aḻukaṇṇi 37–38); outward worship with books, lamps and cakras is lower than the Siddhars' Meru (Caṭṭaimuṉi 1); the homeless realized need no hymns (Kuṭampai 30).

relations.note: rejects outer worship as a path in its own right; contrast Siddhānta

name: The Siddhar critique of pilgrimage and holy bathing

definitions.definition: Karma does not go by visiting Kāśī or bathing in the Gaṅgā (Kaṭuveḷi 15, 33); temples and tanks are within the mind (Sivavākkiyar).

name: The Siddhar critique of scripture and learning

definitions.definition: The four Vedas cry out but cannot see the secret (Pattirakiriyār 48); abiding alone means leaving Vedānta and Veda (32); recitation without inner knowledge is empty (Sivavākkiyar); learning, śāstra and purāṇa are scorned (Pāmbāṭṭi).

Recorded faithfully: the renouncer-poets portray desire for women as a snare and the female body as filth (Paṭṭiṉattār; Pattirakiriyār 8 'thinking of woman as mother'), while the supreme is worshipped as the goddess Vālai/Maṉōṉmaṇi and some Siddhar ritual involved a woman (restricted).

name: The eighteen Siddhars (patiṉeṇ cittarkaḷ) — the lists

definitions.definition: (1) The popular list (widely printed, with samādhi places): Nandi (Kāśī), Agastya (Anantaśayanam), Tirumūlar (Chidambaram), Bogar (Palani), Koṅkaṇar (Tirupati), Maccamuṉi (Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam), Kōrakkar (Poyyūr), Caṭṭaimuṉi (Srirangam), Cuntarāṉantar (Madurai), Rāmatēvar (Aḻakar malai), Kuṭampai (Māyavaram), Karuvūrār (Karūr), Iṭaikkāṭar (Tiruvaṇṇāmalai), Kamalamuṉi (Tiruvārūr), Patañjali (Rāmēśvaram), Taṉvantiri (Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil), Vālmīki (Eṭṭukkuṭi), Pāmbāṭṭi (Caṅkaraṉkōyil). Names moderate, places low confidence.

(2) The Tirumantiram's own lineage lists (checked locally): Nandi's eight — the four Nandis, Śivayoga, Patañjali, Vyāghrapāda and Tirumūlar (TM 67) — and Tirumūlar's mantra-line — Mālāṅkaṉ, Intiraṉ, Cōmaṉ, Piramaṉ, Uruttiraṉ, Kanturu, Kālāṅki, Kañcamalaiyaṉ (TM 69).

(3) The poets of the printed Siddhar anthologies, largely absent from list (1): Sivavākkiyar, Paṭṭiṉattār, Pattirakiriyār, Aḻukaṇṇi, Kaṭuveḷi, Kuṭampai, Pāmbāṭṭi, Iṭaikkāṭar, Akappēy, with works ascribed to Tirumūlar, Caṭṭaimuṉi, Rāmatēvar and Tiruvaḷḷuvar (the local Project Madurai series checked).

(4) Other lists (not reconstructed here) add or substitute names such as Kākapucuṇṭar, Urōmarisi, Pulippāṇi, Tēraiyar, Yūkimuṉi, Kālāṅki, Pulastiyar, Sivavākkiyar and Paṭṭiṉattār; the number eighteen is conventional and the membership varies from source to source.
Tāyumāṉavar praises the 'host of Siddhas' (cittarkaṇam) who attained the harmony of Vedānta and Siddhānta.

notes: The hallucination sweep should check list (1) against printed sources (e.g. the Abhidhāna Cintāmaṇi, Zvelebil's 'The Poets of the Powers') and record the variant lists it finds.

definitions.definition: Nandi's grace made eight masters (nātar) — the four Nandis, Śivayoga, Patañjali, Vyāghrapāda and Tirumūlar (67); by Nandi's grace he received the name nātar and sought Mūlaṉ (68); his mantra-line has seven (listing eight names, 69); four became masters of the four directions and received all he had received (70).

relations.note: the Siddhānta's inner lineage from Nandi

name: The guru in the Siddha tradition

definitions.definition: The guru comes of his own accord to the one who longs, shows his own form and burns the six supports, letters and principles (Aḻukaṇṇi 33–36); the seeker must find the master and bow at his feet (Pattirakiriyār 26); guru and Lord are one, and seeing the Lord as guru is the unspoken mantra (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6); the gaze on the guru makes one a teacher (5); the silent guru teaches by stillness (Tāyumāṉavar). Alchemy and medicine are to be learned only from a guru; hence the code language.

relations.note: Siddhānta: Śiva comes as the guru

name: How Siddha medicine was transmitted (the tradition's account)

definitions.definition: Śiva taught Pārvatī; the knowledge passed through Nandi to the Siddhars, above all Agastya, who taught it to his disciples (Tēraiyar, Pulastiyar and others) and set it in Tamil verse; the texts were veiled in code language and passed from guru to disciple, later in palm-leaf manuscripts held by families of physicians.
